title: Selcan Aydin
text:
Hey, I’m glad you’re here — thanks for stopping by!
I’m a computational scientist at The Jackson Laboratory in Bar Harbor, Maine, working in the Munger Lab. My research sits at the intersection of quantitative genetics, systems biology, and developmental biology, with a focus on how genetic variation shapes gene regulation and cell fate decisions in mice.
Get in touch by sending me an email!

title: Selcan Aydin
text:
About me
Computational biologist with interdisciplinary roots — from mathematical modeling of cell signaling to systems genetics of development.
I grew up in Istanbul, Turkey, and my scientific journey has taken me from modeling biochemical networks in Heidelberg, to mapping the genetics of stress responses in yeast at Duke, to studying how genetic variation reshapes gene regulatory networks in mouse stem cells and their differentiated progeny.
Early in my career I realized that I thrive on interdisciplinary questions. My master’s at Heidelberg introduced me to mathematical modeling of cellular signaling, and my PhD at Duke extended this curiosity to genetic variation — asking how differences in DNA sequence alter the way cells respond to environmental signals. Along the way I picked up a broad toolkit: high-throughput phenotyping, fluorescence and luminescence microscopy, quantitative genetics methods, and computational skills for handling large sequencing datasets. That training planted the seeds of my career as a computational geneticist.

Ph.D. in Biology · Duke University · 2017
M.Sc. in Systems Biology · Universität Heidelberg · 2010
B.Sc. in Biological Sciences & Bioengineering · Sabancı University · 2009


Research at JAX
At JAX I use Diversity Outbred (DO) mice as a resource for systems genetics, mapping how genetic variation shapes gene regulation across multiple molecular layers and cell states. This work traced a causal path from a single regulatory variant near Lifr through a cascade of molecular changes to pluripotency maintenance (Skelly, Czechanski, Byers, Aydin et al., Cell Stem Cell, 2020; Ortmann, Brown, Czechanski, Aydin et al., Cell Stem Cell, 2020), and showed that jointly integrating chromatin, transcript, and protein data uncovers loci invisible to single-omics approaches (Aydin et al., Cell Genomics, 2023). Expanding to neural progenitor cells revealed both conserved and cell-state-specific eQTL, and demonstrated that genetic effects established in ESCs can propagate to shape transcriptional variation in downstream differentiated cells (Aydin et al., G3, 2025; Aydin et al., preprint, 2025). We also released QTLretrievR to make molecular QTL mapping more accessible to the community.
I’m currently applying these approaches to single-cell RNA-seq data and extending our systems genetics framework to new biological contexts, including the developing palate. One thing that has remained constant across all of this work is a genuine love of learning — both picking up new computational methods as the field evolves, and deepening my understanding of the biology along the way.


Teaching, mentoring & outreach
I am passionate about lowering barriers to computational biology for life scientists — especially skills that people find intimidating, like statistics, coding, or working with large datasets. Because most of my own computational skills were self-taught, I know firsthand the value of accessible, well-scaffolded training. I am a certified Posit (RStudio) Tidyverse Instructor and a certified Software Carpentry instructor, and I have been teaching workshops both within JAX and across the broader community.
Beyond the classroom, I am committed to making science a more equitable and welcoming place. I served on the Accessibility Subcommittee of the GSA Early Career Scientist Committees, working to identify barriers faced by scientists with disabilities and develop resources to make research, labs, and conferences more accessible. I have also been active in supporting foreign researchers navigating visa and immigration challenges — an issue close to my own experience as an international scientist — and in raising awareness around mental health in academia.
Outside of work I enjoy hiking, gardening, and spending time with my family and our dog Darwin. 🌿

Hello! I’m a computational scientist at The Jackson Laboratory in Bar Harbor, Maine. Originally from Istanbul, Turkey, I completed my Ph.D. in Biology at Duke University, studying the impacts of genetic variation on cellular phenotypes in budding yeast. My work now focuses on systems genetics — understanding how genetic variation shapes cell fate decisions and mouse development. Outside the lab I enjoy hiking the Maine coast, gardening, and spending time with my family and our dog Darwin. 🌿

title: Dissecting the Effects of Genetic Variation on Stress Response
text: In nature, yeast grow in different niches ranging from trees to people and experience variability in osmolarity. Thus, one might expect to see large variation in the dynamics of osmo-adaptation (phenotype) across different strains (genotype) from diverse environments — and that is exactly what we found.

title: Dissecting the Effects of Genetic Variation on Stress Response
text:
Methods

High-throughput phenotyping pipeline for yeast strains in liquid and solid media
Genetic mapping via bulk segregant analysis and whole genome sequencing (BSAseq)
Multi-parental mapping population building with yeast strains

title: Dissecting the Effects of Genetic Variation on Stress Response
text:
Key Findings
Substantial heritable variation exists in the dynamics of osmo-adaptation across yeast strains. Genetic mapping revealed multiple loci influencing signaling speed, amplitude, and adaptation time — connecting natural genetic variation to dynamic phenotypes.

title: Genetic variation influences pluripotency
text:
In my postdoctoral research at The Jackson Laboratory, I explored the influence of genetic variation on the stability of ground-state pluripotency using mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs).
As part of a multi-investigator collaboration, we used genetic mapping on chromatin accessibility, transcript, and protein abundance in a panel of ESCs derived from hundreds of genetically diverse mice. This work reveals how genetic background shapes the molecular landscape of pluripotency.

title: Genetic variation influences pluripotency
text:
In my postdoctoral research at The Jackson Laboratory, I explored the influence of genetic variation on the stability of ground-state pluripotency using mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs).
As part of a multi-investigator collaboration, we used genetic mapping on chromatin accessibility, transcript, and protein abundance in a panel of ESCs derived from hundreds of genetically diverse mice. This work reveals how genetic background shapes the molecular landscape of pluripotency.

title: Genetic variation influences pluripotency
text:
Methods

Differential gene expression analysis
Multi-omic integration of chromatin, transcript, and protein data
Quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping
Mediation analysis

title: Genetic variation influences pluripotency
text:
Key Findings
Genetic background significantly influences the maintenance of ground-state pluripotency. Distinct loci affect chromatin accessibility, transcript abundance, and protein levels — often independently — revealing a layered genetic architecture underlying cell identity.
My findings also highlight the power of multi-omics data integration in revealing the distal impacts of genetic variation. While QTL mapping with individual traits may be limited due to noise introduced by measurement error, data integration can act to consolidate the influence of genetic signals shared across molecular traits and increase detection power.

title: Mathematical Modeling of Cellular Signaling
text:
My early career training was rooted in systems biology, particularly mathematical modeling of biological processes. Under the supervision of Prof. Dr. Ursula Kummer at the Bioquant Research Institute, University of Heidelberg, I modeled the tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα)-induced activation of NFκB signaling.
Using quantitative data from primary murine hepatocytes, I built and validated an ordinary differential equation (ODE) model of the signaling pathway, estimating kinetic parameters and analyzing sensitivity to perturbations.

title: Mathematical Modeling of Cellular Signaling
text:
My early career training was rooted in systems biology, particularly mathematical modeling of biological processes. Under the supervision of Prof. Dr. Ursula Kummer at the Bioquant Research Institute, University of Heidelberg, I modeled the tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα)-induced activation of NFκB signaling.
Using quantitative data from primary murine hepatocytes, I built and validated an ordinary differential equation (ODE) model of the signaling pathway, estimating kinetic parameters and analyzing sensitivity to perturbations.

title: Mathematical Modeling of Cellular Signaling
text:
Methods

ODE-based mathematical modeling of signaling cascades
Parameter estimation from quantitative time-course data
Parameter sensitivity analysis
Experimental data from primary murine hepatocytes

title: Mathematical Modeling of Cellular Signaling
text:
Key Findings
The model successfully recapitulated dynamic NFκB activation patterns observed experimentally and identified key parameters controlling signal amplitude and oscillation frequency — providing mechanistic insight into how hepatocytes process inflammatory signals.

title: Single-Cell Analysis Reveals Mechanisms of Gene Regulation
text:
Through a collaboration with the Proft Pascual-Ahuir lab, I studied the mechanisms of dose-dependent gene regulation in response to environmental stimuli.
I measured nutrient stress response in single yeast cells using phase and luminescence microscopy combined with microfluidics, enabling precise control of stimulus concentration and timing at the single-cell level.

title: Single-Cell Analysis Reveals Mechanisms of Gene Regulation
text:
Through a collaboration with the Proft Pascual-Ahuir lab, I studied the mechanisms of dose-dependent gene regulation in response to environmental stimuli.
I measured nutrient stress response in single yeast cells using phase and luminescence microscopy combined with microfluidics, enabling precise control of stimulus concentration and timing at the single-cell level.

title: Single-Cell Analysis Reveals Mechanisms of Gene Regulation
text:
Methods

Single-cell luminescence and phase microscopy
Microfluidic device design and operation
Time-series image analysis and quantification
Statistical modeling of dose–response relationships in R

title: Single-Cell Analysis Reveals Mechanisms of Gene Regulation
text:
Key Findings
Single-cell data showed that the graded dose-response behavior of gene expression in response to nutrient stress resulted from the heterogeneous delay in induction. In comparison to osmotic stress where the duration of the induction was shown to be responsible for the graded dose-response. Together, these findings showed that gradual dose-response can be achieved via different regulation principles in budding yeast.
The work here is an early demonstration of the power of single-cell measurements and a significant contribution to the field of cellular signaling furthering our understanding of gene regulation.
